Basics of Questguard RPG.Welcome!:
Well met, adventurer! ..., you are in the right place! In this guide you will find all about roleplaying and Questguard - how to create a character, how to play the game, a glossary of all rules and a section with several tips for Quest Masters.
Warning - This Intro section is still heavily Work In Progress.
Basics of Questguard RPG.Groups (and our community):
Questguard has a dedicated community on Discord where we always organize new campaigns and sessions for players both new and old.
Hit Play With Us! in the upper corner of the menu to see our Discord, and find people to play with!
Basics of Questguard RPG.Learning the rules:
If you never played a Table-Top Roleplaying Game, we recommend you watch this video, to get a grasp of what QuestGuard is: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2PEt5RdNHNw
If you want to try Questguard specifically and you have experience with Dungeons and Dragons (5th edition or One D&D), see the Transition Guide (From D&D)" page, in the Learn To Play menu. It will provide you an easy introduction to Questguard from a D&D perspective.
If you never played a tabletop RPG but you have friends who have played Dungeons and Dragons, send them a link to the "D&D to CoH transition guide" page!
If you decide to play online, there are several platforms for playing Questguard that simulate real life tables with miniatures, dice, music, etc. As of 2023, the most popular such platform is Roll20 (https://roll20.net). It is free for all players and Quest Masters alike and supports many roleplaying games, including Questguard.

The complete new player guide is currently TODO/Work In Progress.

Stats and Attributes.Stats:
There are 4 Stats in QuestGuard, and these reflect your strengths and weaknesses: Might (physical strength, pain tolerance, show of dominance, and confidence), Instinct (running speed, agility, reflexes, and connection to your primal side), Focus (knowledge, talent for magic, resilience of mind, and concentration), Presence (charisma, attunement to the surrounding world, and attention to detail).
Each of these 4 Stats affects a Combat Attribute of your Hero.
- "Might: Increases your maximum Health (3 × Might)."
- "Instinct: Increases your Movement Speed (0.5 for each Instinct)."
- "Focus: Increases your Initiative (0.5 for each Focus)"
- "Presence: Increases your Health Regen after Combats (2 × Presence)."

Your baseline Stat numbers are -1/0/1/2, but increase every Level.
Stats and Attributes.Stat Limit:
The baseline Stat limit is 2, and increases by 1 every 3 Levels (3 for Levels 1 to 3, 4 for Levels 4 to 6, 5 for Levels 7 to 9, and unlimited from Level 10).
You may not go above the Stat Limit in any way, other than with buffs, magic items, and Abilities that explicitly say they can go over the Stat Limit.
Otherwise, if your Stat would be increased above the Stat Limit, nothing happens and the bonus is lost.

Golden Rules of Questguard.1. Rule of Common Presence:
When in doubt about a ruling or if a text leaves something up to interpretation, apply common sense.
The Quest Master has the final say, and may apply the Rule of Cool instead.
Golden Rules of Questguard.2. Always Round Down:
The final number of all calculations is always rounded down (if it's positive).
At no point are calculations intended to take decimals into account, even if several multiplications happen.
Golden Rules of Questguard.2B. Ignore Fractions:
The game may have fractions in certain numbers, most commonly some numbers may have a ".5" (for example, 2.5 or 0.5, or even -1.5).
Whenever you encounter such a number, simply ignore the extra digits after the dot: 2.5 becomes 2, 0.5 becomes 0, and -1.5 becomes -1.
Golden Rules of Questguard.3. Rule of Calling Out:
Some Abilities have effects that happen randomly, at the roll of a die, or apply generally. In gaming, the moment such an effect happens is usually called a "proc".
To keep the game fast, a player is responsible for calling out procs, percentages increases or decreases, etc. If a "proc" happens but nobody notices it, it does not apply if they remember about it too late.
Keep track of your "procs", bonuses and triggered effects! If you forget to use them, you lose them!
The same should apply for the Quest Masters - avoid remembering later that a monster forgot to use one of its Abilities, unless you really, really have to.
Golden Rules of Questguard.4. Teamwork:
Heroes should be adventurers who are eager to go explore, solve mysteries and defeat monsters.
Play together! You win together, as a team. Share responsibilities, spotlights, and distribute loot fairly.

Free Roleplaying.Scenes:
The adventure might be divided into scenes. A Scene might represent players being in a town, exploring a forest, walking down a road, etc.
In a Scene, each Hero has 1 or more Roleplay Action Points, which they can spend to choose to do something (e.g. go shopping, go talk to someone, explore the outskirts, etc).
Each player takes turns round the table doing one Free Roleplay Action, one by one. After players no longer have any Free Roleplay Action Points, the scene ends.

It is up to the Quest Master do determine how many Roleplay Action Points the players have. This can range from 1 Free Roleplay Action Point per player for shorter scenes (or when players have limited time), to 3 or even more Free Roleplay Action Points.
If not sure how many Free Roleplay Action Points to give, 2 is a good number!
Free Roleplaying.Free Roleplay Actions: A player can spend 1 Free Roleplay Action Point to do something that takes time. Usually, spending a Free Roleplay Action Point consists of going somewhere, talking to someone, making non-Combat Rolls, etc.
Free Roleplaying.Rolls (Checks):
A non-Combat Roll is a 2d6 die roll - you roll 2 6-sided dice to determine how well you do, and you add any modifiers you have to that.
If the Quest Master tells you to make a Might Roll, you will roll 2d6 and add your Might stat to the result.
If you have any specific non-Combat Skills, you can add those to the roll if they apply.

Rolling doubles means somoene will get a Plot Point!

Generally, a Check's required number will depend on its difficulty, as established by the Quest Master, requiring at least a number to pass:
- Trivial: 4
- Easy: 7
- Medium: 10
- Hard: 13
- Very Hard: 16
And so on.

The Quest Master is free to change the required number based on the task a Hero wants to achieve
Free Roleplaying.Rolling Doubles for Plot Points:
Whenever a Worthy* Check rolls equal numbers, that Check will produce a Plot Point, either for the Quest Master or the players as a group, whether or not the Check succeeded.
If the Check was a success, the player group gains a Plot Point, which they can spend later.
If it was a failure, the Quest Master gains a Plot Point.
Free Roleplaying.Plot Points:
Players can decide together to spend a Plot Point to do one of the following:
- Introduce an _actually_ fact to the current situation

The Quest Master can spend a Plot Point to do one of the following:
- Introduce an _actually_ fact to the current situation
- Fast-forward time in a way condusive to the plot
- Introduce other complications
In dire need, the Quest Master may also use Plot Points to cancel the effects of a player's Plot Point, but this should be done sparingly.
Free Roleplaying.Plot Points: Actually Fact: To introduce an _actually_ fact to the current situation, spend a Plot Point and simply make a statement starting with "Actually". The fact must be reasonable, fitting, and approved by the Quest Master. The fact can not instantly solve the encounter, and the Quest Master may twist it slightly. Facts can introduce regular physical objects to the scene, ammend a small mistake or oversight, introduce a connection between two characters, or even alter names, looks, or similar traits of people or places. Facts can not be used to correct the results of dice. Here are some examples of facts for the players: - Actually, there is a tree between me and the enemy. - Actually, I did buy that Health Potion from the shop. - Actually, my Hero and this person know eachother. - Actually, I didn't jump the cliff and fail, I stopped right before. - Actually, the name of this NPC is actually Leonard Jackson. For the Quest Master, a fact can also introduce a complication, or force a character to act according to their backstory and quirks. Here are some examples of facts for the Quest Master: - Actually, the place is more heavily guarded than it seemed. - Actually, when falling down the cliff, you further injure your arm. - Actually, your character is afraid to approach the strange man. Note that the Quest Master shouldn't use facts to actively hurt the players, but to introduce interesting plot ramifications! There are plenty of ways to introduce truths, and ultimately, the Quest Master has the final word on whethere a fact is accepted.
Free Roleplaying.Plot Points: Fast Forward: The Quest Master may spend a Plot Point to advance time outside of Combat. The time advanced this way must be proportional to the current pacing of the game. For example, if the pacing of the situation is by the minute, the Quest Master can force a time skip of a few minutes (e.g. when the players are actively haggling with a vendor, or are engaged in a discussion going nowhere). If the passing pacing is more slow, the Quest Master may skip time to advance the plot faster (e.g. when exploring the country side, shopping for items, etc). The primary use of the fast-forward is to skip over time that is not meaningful to the plot, can not result in a positive scenario, or is derailing the adventure. In certain conditions, doing a time-skip can be used to end a Combat early, but only when the result of the Combat is already clear. Here are some examples of fast-forwarding: - Fasting forward, you finished shopping for goods and are now in the town square. - Fasting forward, this conversation lead no where and you were seen out by the guards. - Fasting forward, you kept investigating the room and found no extra evidence, and are now outside. - Fasting forward, the Combat ended in a clear victory and you are now in camp, having collected the valuable materials from the monster.
Free Roleplaying.NPC Suspicion:
Interacting with non-player characters (NPC's) may be freeform, up to the QuestMaster's leisure, but there is a rule on how players will interact with NPC's.
Each NPC has a level of Suspicion: the higher their Suspicion, the harder it is to convince them of something.
Whenever a player makes a Check to convince an NPC about something, they must roll at least equal to their Suspicion. If they succeed, the Suspicion is reduced. Otherwise, it increases.
The numbers for this are currently work in progress (WIP), but you're free to try it out!
Free Roleplaying.Social Etiquette:
Be nice and don't interrupt others; try to make decisions as a team.
Wait for your turn, unless given permission by other players and the Quest Guard to have priority.

Crafting.Crafting Basics:
A craftsman can craft an item for a total price equal to its regular cost, but it can take 1 up to 7 days (in-game) depending on the item crafted.
You can order a custom crafted regular item with a different look!

You can provide the crafter with materials worth an amount of Gold, which will be subtracted from the original cost.
Crafting.Crafting Components:
A craftsman can take extra Crafting Components to add to the item to create a custom Magic Item for an extra 200 Gold.
Crafting components are objects that add properties to items, such as a Weapon Component - Poison Gland (converts Damage to Poison for weapons).
Crafting Components are usually obtained from slain monsters or found in the wild.
Crafting.Price of Crafting Components:
Adding only one Crafting Component to a crafting order costs 150 Gold. After that, each extra Component costs twice as much.

Adding 1 Component costs 150 Gold.
Adding 2 Components costs 300 Gold (150 * 2).
Adding 3 Components costs 600 Gold (300 * 2).
Adding 4 Components costs 1200 Gold (600 * 2).
And so on.

You can find these prices at the Game menu, under the Other section, on the Shop & Prices page.
Crafting.Harvesting Components:
Harvesting regular Components may require a Roll above 10.
Getting doubles may instead let you harvest a Rare Component.
Each monster's harvestable parts can be found in its Loot section.

Player Tools.Character Sheets: You can find all types of Character Sheets (PDF, PNG, PSD) under Game > Other.
Player Tools.Ability Tracker (Online):
For keeping track of all your Abilities, you can use the Ability Tracker tool, which should be self explanatory.
You can find it at the Game menu, under the Abilities section, on the Ability Sheet Maker page.
You can save these by saving the URL of the page. Whenever you make a modification to the sheets, the URL changes automatically. Make sure you have backups!

Combat.Combat By Turns:
Tactical combat is a large part of what makes Questguard fun and interesting!

During Combat, players and monsters take Turns.
Combat.Turn Order (Initiative):
Warning: The rules for turn Order are still being tested and are TODO/WIP.

Players take Turns clockwise (or counter-clockwise), starting from the left-most player (though the order rules are still being tested and are work-in-progress).

Enemy groups take turns inbetween players. All Enemies of a type act at the same time.
Combat.Monster Setback:
Monsters have an extra Attribute that Heroes don't - Setback.
A monster's Setback represents after how many Heroes Turns the monster may take its Turn.

For example, a monster with 1 Setback takes its Turn after the first Hero finished its Turn this Round.
A monster with 3 Setback takes its Turn after the 3rd Hero finished its Turn this Round.
A monster with 0 Setback takes its Turn before all Heroes.

If a monster's Setback is higher than the number of players, it just takes its Turn last.

If multiple monsters have the same Setback, they take their Turns at the same time (or in any order).
Combat.Ambushing:
If the Hero party catches a monster party by surprise, each member of the Hero party can make a Check for stealth (difficulty may vary from situation to situation).
For each success, monsters get +1 Setback this fight. However, any failure cancels this bonus. Be careful who wishes to ambush!

If a monster party catches the players by surprise, each player makes a Check to see if they are surprised (difficulty may vary).
For each failure, monsters get -1 Setback this fight.
Combat.Retreating:
You can retreat, disengage, or exit Combat by spending 1 Action Point, if you're on the edge of the battlefield.
Once you retreated retreated, your Turn ends, and you can't re-enter Combat until it is finished.

Acts and Actions.Action Points and Actions:
Heroes all have 3 Action Points on their Turn, which they can spend however they like; attacking, casting a magic Spell, or anything you can think of that uses your hands (usually).

Moving a number of meters up to your Movement Speed takes 1 Action Point.
Attacking, casting Spells, or doing other Acts take a varying number of Action Points, depending on the Ability or weapon. This cost is written explicitly on all Abilities and weapons in the game.
Think of 1 Action Point as doing something that requires only 1 Hand. Attacking with a Dagger only costs 1 Action Point, but attacking with a Greatsword costs 2 Action Points, because you need both hands.

But it gets better! You don't actually need to keep track of which hand you used already! It doesn't matter you already used your right hand. 1 Action Point is 1 Action Point. Use them at leisure!
If you have a shield and a One-Handed Sword, yes, you can make 3 attacks with the same hand with the same sword.

There are no diminishing returns for doing the same thing over and over again.
Acts and Actions.Reaction: You have 1 Reaction per Round. Some Abilities allow you to use your Reaction. Otherwise, you have nothing to do with it.
Acts and Actions.Initiative Rundown: On your first Turn each Combat, you have an extra number of Action Points equal to your Initiative.
Acts and Actions.Acts:
Simply put, doing anything willingly on your Turn is considered an Act.
Doing an Act means Moving, using a Reaction or doing anything worth 0 or more Actions. Effects triggered by or through Passives are not considered Acts.
For example, when you Move, that is an Act. Using a the Innervate Spell takes 0 Action Points, so it's an Act. When the Cleric's Passive Spell Awe triggers, that is NOT considered an Act.
Engaging in Roleplay is not considered an Act, unless the Quest Master decides so.
Acts and Actions.Stunts:
A Hero may attempt a Stunt - doing something unconventional to attempt to deal more Damage or apply a certain effect.
For example, if a Player wants to do a falling attack on a monster, or try to burn a specific part of a monster's fur, or shout so hard that rocks fall from the ceiling.

Attempting a Stunt requires a Check.
Passing a Stunt Check might give bonuses such as +50% extra Damage (or even +100% for one-handed weapons), Single-Stunning the target, dealing extra Damage in an Area, Healing for an amount around 1d10, etc.
Failing a Stuns usually means losing the Action Points for that Stunt.
Acts and Actions.Repeating Stunts:
After someone attempts a Stunt, that Stunt may never be repeated in the same party or with the same Quest Master, by anyone in the party, ever.
Ultimately, the Quest Master has the final word on whether a Stunt may or may not be done.

Movement.Movement (Moving):
Every Unit can move in combat. When you see the term "move", "moving", "Movement", etc, that always refers to walking, running, jumping, etc.

Using 1 Action Point, you can move once a number of meters equal to your Speed.

You can't split your Movement around other Acts. For example, if you spend 1 Action Point to move just 1 meter, then decide to do anything (e.g. attack, or even do something free), then want to move again, you must use another Action Point.
Unused Movement is not carried over!
Note that you can freely switch direction while moving, if it's in the same movement. If you want, you can move in one direction for a few meters, do a 180 degree turn and move back. That is valid movement.
Movement.Jumping: As part of your normal Movement, you can freely jump a number of meters equal to your Instinct, without needing a Check.
Movement.Slamming or Pushing:
Some Abilities "Slam", "push" or "pull" Units (pulling is just pushing in the opposite direction).
When a Unit is Slammed, pushed, teleported, etc (or when you do it to yourself), it does not cost 1 Action Point. If an Ability says a Unit "moves a number of meters...", it does not use Action Points unless it explicitly says so. Slamming or pushing a Unit does not consume that Unit's movement.

A Unit may use a Reaction to grab onto a ledge or object when Slammed or pushed. They stop and, if Slammed, take the Slam Damage as if they hit an obstacle where they stop.
Movement.Opportunity Attacks: There are no opportunity attacks in Quest Guard. Movement usually has no penalties.
Movement.Turning Around:
On your Turn, you can freely turn around and face any direction at any point. Turning is not considered an Act and does not count as Movement.
Turning can only be done inbetween other Acts. You can't' turn while doing another Act.
Movement.Other Movement:
Jumping takes away from Movement meters, whether vertical or horizontal.
So, if you decide to jump 1 meter ahead, this still takes 1 meter of movement, as it normally would (the QM might make you roll a Check for succeeding the jump, though).
Climbing a 2 meter wall takes 2 meters out of your movement. If you are jumping both horizontally and vertically, you only use the movement for the horizontal movement (e.g. if you jump to a ledge 1 meter away that's 1 meter tall, this only uses 1 meter; similarly, if you are jumping to a ledge 3 meters away that's 2 meters tall, this takes only 3 meters out of your movement).
Movement.Moving Through Units:
You can move normally through Allied Units' spaces. Only Units smaller in size can move through enemy Units of a larger size (e.g. Small may move through Medium, Medium may move through Large, etc).
For them, those spaces underneath the larger Unit count as Hard Terrain.
Movement.Hard Terrain:
Moving inside a Hard Terrain space take 2 meters instead of 1.
Moving outside of Hard Terrain to normal terrain costs 1 meter of movement, as normal.

Combat Encounter & Units.Combat Encounter: When you want to fight, the game switches from free roleplay to combat.
Combat Encounter & Units.Unit:
Any acting person, monster or creature is considered a Unit (e.g. it's not inanimate and can take turns).
Inanimate objects can be considered Units only if and when you're targeting or affecting them with attacks or Abilities, and it's necessary that they be considered Units (e.g. for certai special effects).
The QM has the final say in whether something is a Unit or not.
Combat Encounter & Units.Ally vs Enemy:
A friendly Unit is considered an Ally. A hostile Unit is considered an Enemy.
Inanimate Unit objects are considered neither Allies, nor Enemies.
Combat Encounter & Units.Worthiness (Worthy Enemy):
Worthiness describes whether something is done in good faith within the fiction of the game, rather than for a mechanical meta-game advantage.
Something is Worthy if it fits the narrative context and is not done primarily to gain an unintended mechanical advantage.
Anything can be Worthy (a Worthy reason), but the 2 most common uses are for Worthy Combat and Worthy Enemies. A Worthy Enemy is a normal enemy that tries to kill you during a combat encounter only.
Certain Abilities specify that they only work against "Worthy Enemies".

The following are ^not^ considered Worthy:
- Defenseless Units (e.g. civillians, hunted deer, etc) and Units that don't attack or don't want to attack
- Non-Units (e.g. air, the ground, a tree, etc)
- Temporarily equipping an magical armor to gain a roleplay advantage, then unequipping it immediately after
- "Time-skip combats" (quick combat, encounters resolved through roleplaying, etc)
- A character's name that is clearly intended as a joke
- Every single creature in a swarm (e.g. a single bat is not a Worthy Enemy, but a Bat Swarm as a Unit is)

Apply common sense. Ultmately, the Quest Master has the final word on whether something is Worthy or not, and may forbid certain non-Worthy situations. Note that this should not be done to railroad the players and force them on a certain path, but to keep the story believable, immersive, and prevent unintended meta-gaming situations.
Combat Encounter & Units.Unit Sizes:
Medium and smaller Units occupy a 1x1 meter space.
Large Units occupy a 2x2 meter space. It is up to the QM to tell how much space a Unit larger than Large occupies, and how well it can fit through gaps and units.
When moving a Large Unit (or larger), count the number of meters it moved from the center of its starting space to the center of its end space.

If someone is a smaller size than another Unit, that someone may move through the space of that Unit as if it were Hard Terrain.

Hitting only one space of a Large or larger Unit with an Area Ability is perfectly valid (has no special penalties, deals full Damage as if it hit fully, etc).
Combat Encounter & Units.Carrying Units: A Unit carrying another Unit is Slowed (and might not be able to use its hands, depending on the situation).
Combat Encounter & Units.Mounted Combat & Riding:
A Unit can spend 1 Action Point to mount or dismount another Unit at least one size larger than you. The mounted Unit can spend 1 Action Point to freely unmount the rider.
Most Units can be mounted or ridden, but unless it is Ridable (specifically purposed as a Mount), a mount is Slowed.

If the mount is Ridable, your two Turns are merged into a regular one and act together as a singular Unit (you have 3 Action Points and can control what the mount does, with your own Action Points). A mount usually provides higher Movement Speed and may have other useful Abilities.
The Ridable mount is immune to Damage from outside and can't be targeted. However, all the final Damage the rider takes (after all calculations) is also done directly to the mount, ignoring the mount's Resistances or Weaknesses or similar effects.
Simply put, you and your mount always take the same Damage.

If the mount dies, the rider unmounts and is Single-Stunned.
Apply common sense to whether a Unit is Ridable, can attack its rider, the rider has Cover from its mount, etc. Slamming, pushing, or teleporting may or may not take the mount with the rider (and viceversa), up to the Quest Master.

Damage & Status.Damage Rundown:
The Damage usually works on the principle of "what you see is what you get".
Usually, there are no Damage reductions like Armor. You deal the Damage you see on the dice
Damage & Status.Offensive Ability/Attack:
An Attack or Offensive Ability is something that deals Damage or inflicts a Control Effect, coming directly from a Unit through a missile, weapon or direct Spell.
Delayed Damage sources are not considered Attacks (e.g. Damage over time)

The Hail Spell is an attack. Magic Arrows counts as multiple attacks. Curse of Pain's Damage is not an attack.
The term "attack" is relevant for some Abilities.
The term "attack" is also sometimes used to simply refer to the Act of hitting or striking a Unit (e.g. making a melee attack). A "weapon attack" is simply the Act of attacking with a weapon.
The terms "attack" and "Offensive Act" are used interchangeably, though this will be streamlined in the near future (TODO/WIP).
Damage & Status.Damage and Damage Types:
Damage is a word for how many Health Points an attack or effect will reduce. Dealing 3 Damage to a Unit with 10 Health will leave the Unit at 7 Health. Upon reaching 0 or less Health, a Unit dies or Falls (see Death and being Fallen).
There are multiple "types" of Damage, but this is just a classification for certain Abilities, and usually 3 Damage is 3 Damage, no matter the type.
The Damage types are:
- Slash
- Smash
- Pierce
- Pulse (pressure)
- Fire
- Cold
- Shock
- Scourge (dark, necrotic, eldritch)
- Divine
- Psychic
- True*
There are Passive Abilities ("Resistances") that reduce certain Damage types you take by 50%, or increase it by 50% ("Weaknesses").

True Damage can not be mitigated, ignores Shielding (deals directly Damage to Health) and regular Damage reductions and Resistances. There are, however, some Abilities that can reduce True Damage, but they are very rare.
If a Unit has Shielding or similar effects, True Damage directly affects Health. The Shielding is not consumed.
Damage & Status.Damage Calculation Order: The order for calculating Damage is always additions/subtractions first, and then percentages. The order in which Damage is added or subtracted from an Attack is: 1. Add or subtract all flat attack modifiers (e.g. curses, bonuses from buffs, etc). 2. Calculate all percentages (e.g. Blind -50%, Frail +50%, etc). Percentages are additive (see Percentages). 3. Subtract at most 1 Shielding
Damage & Status.Percentages:
All percentage calculations are additive, meaning taking +50% Damage from a source and another +50% Damage from another source results in taking +100% Damage.
The final result is always rounded down. Individual percentages are not calculated separately, but instead only the final percentage is calculated.

For example, let's say you Attack a Unit with a Handgun and you roll 8. Your attack is Blinded, the enemy has one Shielding that can block 2 Damage, takes +50% Pierce Damage, has Cover, and you are using special Bullets that deal +1 Damage.
The Damage becomes:
1. 8 + 1 (from bullets) - 2 (from Shielding) = 7
2. 100% of 7 + 50% of 7 (from the Pierce weakness) - 50% of 7 (from Cover) - 50% of 7 (from Blinded)
The +50% and -50% cancel out: 100% of 7 - 50% of 7 (from Blinded) = 50% of 7 = 3 (because we round down only the final result).

Note that for this step with percentages we do not calculate the result of each percentage individually, but we simply subtract or add to 100% to get the final percentage. Only at the end do we calculate the final number.
Damage & Status.Shielding:
A Unit may have one or more Shieldings that can block an amount of Damage.
The next time the Unit takes Damage, they must subtract exactly one of the Shieldings from the Damage being taken, then that Shielding is lost.

If it has at laast one Shielding, the Unit must block Damage with one of their Shieldings, whichever they choose.
Only one Shielding may be used to block Damage at a time. Shieldings do not stack on top of one-another.

When an Ability says something akin to "someone gets a Shielding that can block 1d6 Damage", roll the Shielding at that moment and keep the die to represent the Shielding on that character.
Damage & Status.Spellpower:
Some Abilities and Items give extra Spellpower on certain Abilities or types of effects.
Extra Spellpower applies as a flat or die bonus to all Damage, Healing, and Shielding done with Abilities.
Spellpower does not apply regular Slams (since it's not magical Damage) or to weapon attacks or if an Ability specifies using a weapon, regardless of the Damage type.

For example, Burning Breath deals 1d6 Damage in a 3x3 meter area. If you have +1 Spellpower, it will do 1d6 + 1 Damage.

Spellpower applies to all of Damage, Healing, and Shielding individually, so Abilities that do both apply the flat bonus to both!
This may be tricky: for example, Blood Dividend (from Warlock) makes your next Spell deal -50% Damage, but heals for the Damage Dealt.
Let's assume you have +1d4 Spellpower and you would deal a total of 10 Damage on that next Spell. That Damage becomes 10 + 1d4. Let's say you roll 2 on the d4, so the Damage becomes 12. You deal 50% of that as Damage (6), then Heal for the Damage dealt (which would be 6). But since Spellpower applies to Healing separately as well, you would do 6 + 1d4 Healing!

Bottom line is: whenever you deal Damage, add Spellpower. Whenever you Heal, add Spellpower, regardless of when or how much. Same goes for Shielding.
Damage & Status.My Health and Mana:
How much you can resist in combat is determined by your Health Points. Every living (or undead) thing in the game has Health Points (or just Health, or HP).
your Hero has a set amount of Health Points determined by how you created your Hero.

Whenever you take Damage, you subtract that many points from your current Health Points.
If someone reaches 0 or less Health Points, they die (or at least Fall incapacitated).

In QuestGuard, you can't take "long rests" to recover Health, but you recover an amount of Health after each Worthy Combat equal to your Health Regen.
At the end of every Adventure, you recover all resources (Health, Mana, etc). The Quest Master will tell you when that happens.
Damage & Status.Being Fallen:
When you get to 0 Health, you become Fallen until you restore Health.

While Fallen, you skip your Turn. If you are Healed, you come back with Exhaustion (see Exhaustion).
Damage & Status.Exhaustion (Combat):
Each rank of Exhaustion reduces your Action Points by 1 per Turn (e.g. Single-Exhaustion means -1 Action Point, Double-Exhaustion means -2 Action Points, etc).

When you become Fallen (reach 0 Health), or when you take Damage while being Fallen, you become Exhausted (Single-Exhausted).

If you are already Exhausted, you become Double-Exhausted.
If you are already Double-Exhausted, you become Triple-Exhausted.
If you are already Triple-Exhausted, you die permanently.

Combat Exhaustion lasts until the end of the Combat.
Damage & Status.Exhaustion (Non-Combat):
You also become Single-Exhausted for each 24 hours without sleep, from overdosing on potions (e.g. if you drink more than 1 potion per hour), or from magical effects.

You cure one rank of Exhaustion (Non-Combat) by sleeping for 8 hours.
Damage & Status.Death: Heroes or Units that behave like Heroes (e.g. become Fallen instead of dying) die when they take Damage when they're already Triple-Exhausted.
Damage & Status.Distace:
When calculating distance from point A to point B, calculate the distance from the square A is on to the square B is on like this:
Start from a square near A and count squares one by one (in a line or diagonally) until you get to B. You also count the square B is on for this.
Remember this by thinking that if A is on the corner of B, that's a distance of 1 meter.
Damage & Status.Range:
To calculate the range from a Unit to another Unit, simply measure the distance from that Unit's space's center to the other Unit's space's center.
If one of the Units is Large or larger, measure the distance from one of its outer-most spaces to the one of the other Unit's outer-most spaces (e.g. for Large Units - NOT to center, but to edge).

An easy way to measure this, if you're playing on a grid, is to count the number of squares from one Unit to another. If the other Unit is in a square right next to his Unit (even diagonally), the distance is 1 meter. If there's an empty square between them, the distance is 2. And so on.
Damage & Status.Minimum / Maximum Range:
Some Abilities and weapons have a minimum and maximum Range (e.g. 3-5 meters).

Attacking below the minimum range has a -50% penalty.
You can not attack beyond the maximum range of a weapon (it is considered you do not have Line of Sight).

Specified ranges are inclusive (e.g. 3-5 meters range means you can attack normally at 3 and 5 meters range).
Damage & Status.Melee vs Ranged:
Abilities usually specify if an attack is considered melee or ranged.
All offensive Acts done within 1 meter are considered melee. All melee weapon attacks or Abilities that use melee weapons are considered melee, even if their range if more than 1 meter.
Otherwise, all other offensive Acts are considered ranged.
Damage & Status.Darkness:
Attacks on Units standing in darkness have Cover (-50% Damage).
The Quest Master will determine if a Unit has Line of Sight through darkness. Apply common sense.
There are, however,
Damage & Status.Recommended Darkness Rules:
In darkness, your Line of Sight is 3 meters.
When you spot a Unit in darkness, everyone may now have Line of Sight to them, unless they move further into the darkness.


If a Unit is standing in light (or is illumintated in some way), anyone may have Line of Sight to it (obviously).                
Certain Spells, items and fire may illuminate areas (e.g. short bursts of fire illuminate an area in 3 meters for up to 6 seconds, aka 1 Round). Naturally, Units can see illuminated areas even if they themselves are standing in darkness.
Certain Abilities may allow Units to see well in the dark up to a specified distance (and as such they have Line of Sight up to that distance, and don't have Cover).
Damage & Status.Line of Sight:
If you can see a Unit directly, you have Line of Sight to it.

To clarify, if Unit A can see Unit B with their bare eyes, then Unit A has Line of Sight to Unit B.
If Unit A can see even a little bit of the body of Unit B, then Unit A still has Line of Sight to Unit B (but attacks usually gain the Cover pentalty, which is -2).

To use an Ability, you need Line of Sight to the center target point of where you are casting the Ability.

If playing on a grid, if you have to target a point, you target the square that point is in. You can't normally target square intersections unless the Ability states you can.
If you target a Unit, you must have Line of Sight to its square.

There is Line of Sight from square A to square B if you can draw a line from any corner of square A to any corner of square B without any other Unit or Obstacle crossing the line.
However, other Units' or obstacles' squares can _intersect_ the line you were drawing if it's merely tangential, and does not pass from one side of the line to the other.
See the example below.

Without magical means, Line of Sight is always 2-way. If Unit A has LoS to Unit B, then Unit B also has LoS to Unit A (assuming they look at one another).
Transparent solid objects (e.g. windows) do not block Line of Sight, but obviously missiles like arrows and magic bolts can't go through them. Apply common sense.

Allies do not block Line of Sight, and neither do Enemies, but attacking a target behind another Unit provides them with Cover against the attack.
Damage & Status.Cover:
An Act (attack, Spell, etc) has Cover if done "through" or over an obstacle or Unit, or Line of Sight is somewhat obstructed (fog, water, etc).
Cover reduces the total roll (or Damage, or Healing, etc) by 50%.
Whether something has Cover is up to the Quest Master's interpretation. It is possible that a Unit has Cover from another Unit, but not necessarily viceversa (e.g. if shooting from behind a rock).
Damage & Status.Area:
For Abilities that affect areas, the distance is calculated to the edge square of the area.
E.g. for a 4x4 meter area, if the range is 6 meters, there should be a path of 5 empty squares between the caster and the area.

If a spell targets a line, it starts from a square right in front of you and continues in a line.
E.g. if the line is 2 meters long, it takes the square in front of you, and the next one.
Damage & Status.Semi-Hitting (Area Abilities):
When playing on a grid, you might sometimes position an area Ability in such way that it somewhat hits certain Units, hits half of their Spaces, or is in an awkward shape.
A fair warning: it is not recommended that you allow awkward area positions on the board.

Semi-Hitting deals -2 Damage and Semi-Hit Units gain +2 to Checks made from it.
For example, you could position a 3x3 meter area in the center of a 4x4 meter area; thus, the 4 squares in the middle will be fully covered by the 3x3 area, but the surrounding squares will all only be covered by a half of a square from the 3x3 area (or even a quarter).

Note: a Large Unit takes the full effect even if only one space (1x1 meter) of its total area is hit (e.g. hitting only a square of the 4 squares of a Large Unit applies the normal effect - it is NOT a Semi-Hit).
Damage & Status.Mass (Damage): Dealing Mass Damage means Damaging multiple Units with the same Act. The same applies to Mass Healing, Mass Crowd Control, etc.
Damage & Status.\"All\" vs \"Each\":
The difference between the terms "all" and "each" in Abilities is intentional:

When you affect "all" (Units) with an effect, you only roll the dice once. If multiple of those Units must roll dice as part of the effect or as a response, each can roll its own dice separately.
When you affect "each" (Unit) with an effect, you roll the dice for each affected.
Damage & Status.Near (Nearness): 'Near' and 'Adjacent' refers to all spaces within 1 meter of a Unit.
Damage & Status.Falling Damage:
Falling inflicts 1d6 Smash Damage for every 2 meters fallen (assuming you land on hard ground).
E.g. falling 3 meters deals 1d6 Damage, falling 4 meters deals 2d6 Damage, 5 meters - 2d6, 6 meters - 3d6, etc.
Having someone fall on you deals the same True Damage to you as it does to the faller.
The Quest Master might reduce the Damage or mitigate it depending what you land on or if you fall onto an enemy with an attack. If you're a Quest Master, consider halving the fall Damage if a Unit falls intentionately on another Unit to attack it.
Damage & Status.Combat & Resist Checks:
Some Abilities require you to make a "Check against something". To succeed, you need to roll a Check equal to or higher than the number you're rolling against. These are called Combat Checks. If you're battling against another Check, you need to roll higher than the enemy Check.
Some monster Abilities will have you make a Resist Check. These are just like normal Checks or Combat Checks. As usual, you must roll equal to or higher than the number you're rolling against in order to succeed.
Damage & Status.Dice Upgrade/Downgrade:
Having Dice Upgraded means, for example, d6's become d8's, or d10's become d12's. D12's and d20's just gain +1.
Dice Downgraded is the opposite, so it means, for example, d8's become d6's, or d10's become d8's. D2's and d20's just gain -1.

Note that Upgrading or Downgrading Dice for an Ability or weapon attack applies to all dice displayed on it! That includes special weapon text like Critical Strikes.

Control Effects.Control Effects standards:
A "Control Effect" is a condition or debuff on a Unit that prevents it from doing things normally (e.g. Stunned means it has fewer Action Points, Slowed means it's harder to move, etc).
all Control Effects lasts until the end of that Unit's next Turn (or until the end of their current Turn if it's their Turn now), unless stated otherwise.
Control Effects of different types stack together (e.g. a Unit can be both Slowed and Blinded).
Most Control Effects of the same type also stack (e.g. if you make a Unit Double-Slowed, its next Move Act will cost +2 Action Points).
Control Effects.Slam:
When a Unit is Slammed a number of meters in a direction, it is pushed that much in that direction.
If it hits another Unit or obstacle, it stops. Calculate how many meters left of the Slamming were left that it should have been pushed if it weren't for the obstacle or Unit.
If it hit an obstacle, the Unit takes that much Smash Damage.
If it it a Unit, they both take half of that as Smash Damage.

Note that any Unit may use a Reaction to grab onto a ledge or object when Slammed. They stop and take the Slam Damage as if they hit an obstacle where they stop.
Control Effects.Lagged: On its next Turn, a Slowed Unit's next Move Act costs 1 extra Action Point for each level of Slow. Also affects Abilties that specify making a Move Act. Until it does, it can't use Reaction Abilities that specify making a Move Act. Other movement Abilities are unaffected (teleports, dashing, leaping, Slamming/Pushing, etc).
Control Effects.Deafened: On its next Turn, a Deafened Unit's next Ability costs 1 extra Action Point (except Reactions and Default Actions). For non-Heroes, this does not affect Abilities that have "Attack" in their name.
Control Effects.Dazed: On its next Turn, a Dazed Unit's weapon attack costs 1 extra Action Point (body parts are considered weapons). Also affects Abilities that specify using a weapon (or body parts). For non-Heroes, this only affects Abilities that have "Attack" in their name.
Control Effects.Stunned:
A Single-Stunned Unit loses 1 Action Point on its next Turn.
A Double-Stunned Unit loses 2 Action points on its next Turn.
A Triple-Stunned Unit loses 3 Action points on its next Turn.

Stunning a Unit multiple times stacks up to Triple-Stunned.
Control Effects.Slowed: A Slowed Unit has -50% Movement Speed on its next Movement Act. Other movement Abilities are unaffected (teleports, dashing, leaping, Slamming/Pushing, etc).
Control Effects.Frailed: Next time the Unit takes Damage, it takes +50%.
Control Effects.Blinded: A Blinded Unit's next Damage or Healing Act does -50% Healing or Damage.
Control Effects.Crippled: A Crippled Unit's next Damage or Healing Act does -100% Healing or Damage.
Control Effects.Silenced: A Silenced Unit can not use any Abilities on its next Turn. Monsters can only use physical attacks that use only 1 Action Point.
Control Effects.Rooted: A Rooted Unit can not use Movement on its next Turn.
Control Effects.Exhaustion (Combat):
When you "Rise From Being Fallen", you come back to life with Exhaustion (Single-Exhaustion), which lasts until the Combat is over.
Each degree of Exhaustion stacks. If you were already Single-Exhausted, you become Double-Exhausted. If you were Double-Exhausted, you become Triple-Exhausted.
While Triple-Exhausted, if you reach 0 Health, you die.

Each level of Exhaustion reduces your Action Points per Turn by 1, and all your Damage, Healing and Rolls by 50%. At Triple-Exhausted, you have -3 Action Points per Turn, deal -150% Damage and Healing and all your Rolls get -150%.

Combat Exhaustion lasts until the end of the Combat.
Control Effects.Other Interactions:
If a Unit gets affected by a Control Effect while doing an Act (e.g. you activate a trap while shooting a bow), what happens depends on the Control Effect type.
If pushed or Slammed, the Unit is Pushed immediately (and dashes are cancelled). If the Act was not started yet (e.g. not yet attacked), then the Unit is free to do something else after being Pushed if they want to. However, if the Act already started (e.g. fired 1 out of 3 Magic Missiles), the Unit must continue casting the Spell, on the same target if it was already chosen, only if it's still valid (e.g. has Line of Sight or Range). If the Act can't be continued due to Range, Line of Sight, etc, then the rest of the Act is cancelled; Actions/Resoureces are NOT regained and are lost.
Cripple, Slow: Nothing happens on the spot; the Control Effect takes effect after the Ability finishes.
Silence: If it's a Spell, the rest of the Spell gets cancelled; otherwise nothing else happens.
Single-Stun and Double-Stun: If the target still has enough Action Points for the Act, it continues. Otherwise, it is cancelled and the Unit may do something else if it still has Action Points.
Triple-Stun and other non-listed strong Control Effect: The Ability gets cancelled.
Becoming Slowed on your turn immediately reduces your remaining Speed by 2 (but not less than 0, obviously).

Weapons and Armor.Critical Strikes:
Many weapons can land Critical Strikes if you roll maximum on one or more dice specified.
If the attack had extra Damage from other sources, and it's the same die type that can roll the required number, then also take that die into account.

For example, the Punch (1d4 Damage) lands a Critical strike if you rolled maximum on the weapon die (which means 4). However, if your attack gains another 1d4 Damage (thus making it 2d4), it will land a Critical Strike if any of the d4's rolled a 4.

If your weapon attack has its Dice Upgraded to the next die type (e.g. from 1d4 to 1d6), then the Critical Strike now happens if you roll 6 on the d6.
Weapons and Armor.Throwing weapons:
If you want to throw a weapon that's not baseline made for throwing, it is considered an Improvised Attack (there's a Default Move Basic Ability called Improvised Attack).
There exists a Feat called Throwing Expert that allows you to throw weapons with their normal Damage.
You still need to be Trained in that weapon to throw it without it being an Improvised Attack.
Weapons and Armor.Swapping Weapons:
At the start of your turn, you can freely choose what weapons to use or swap for the rest of your turn.
For example, when your turn starts, you can choose to prepare one Shortsword and a Shield, or a Greatclub, or a Hand Crossbow and a Dagger.
You can use these weapons however you like on your turn.
If you ever want to swap weapons in the middle of your turn, you must spend 1 Action Point.

Changing weapons at the start of your turn is encouraged! Use different weapons to your advantage!
Weapons and Armor.Aiming:
You can not aim for a specific area when attacking of using an Ability.
However, in niche cases, the Quest Master might allow a Stunt to try to hit a specific point of a Unit.

Abilities.Abilities explained:
An Ability is simply a block of text that either gives you something extra (passively) or gives you something else to do with your Action Points rather than attacking.
Most things in Quest Guard are Abilities: weapons, Spells, Feats, etc.

Abilities have an icon, name, tags for various important things like Cost, Range, etc.
Abilities can be either Passive or active. Passive Abilities give you an effect that is generally applicable, and usually you do not need to "activate" them specifically; they activate on their own.
Active Abilities require Action Points (maybe even 0 Action Points!) in order to activate them manually.
One quick way to differentiate Passive from Active Abilities is that Active Abilities have a square icon, while Passive Abilities have a rounder icon!
Abilities.0 Action Points:
If an Ability costs 0 Action Points, you can use it as many times as your Mana or Cooldown allows.
These are considered an Act.
Abilities.Ability Limit Per Turn: There is no limit to how many Abilities you can use on your Turn.
Abilities.Ability Text:
The base block of text for an Ability is the effect of that Ability - its bread-and-butter. It's written in normal text, and explains simply what the Ability does. The smaller black text below the effect usually provides some extra information, like certain exceptions or cases, or explains some extra rules. The even smaller gray text in italics are the notes of the Ability. These usually provide clarifications for how the Ability works, and sometimes describes the flavor of the Ability.
The easiest way to keep track of your Abilities is to either use the Character Creator on the website (under Create A Character), or with the Ability Sheet Maker, at the Game menu, under Abilities, on the Ability Sheet Maker page.
Abilities.Ability Tags: Written with white text on dark background on small rectangles are the tags of the Ability. These don't add extra information, but are just meant as quick reference to see what kind of Ability it is at a glance.
Abilities.Cooldown:
Some Abilities have a Cooldown.
Cooldown refers to the time you must wait to use the Ability again.

An Ability's Cooldown is represented by the _white hourglass_ icon. If an Ability has no such icon, then it has no Cooldown and can be used as often as you like.
A Cooldown of "Once / Adventure" means you can use the Ability once, and then can't use it again until you finish the current Adventure.

Some Abilities have a Cooldown mentioning "real hours" or other real time. This refers to the real-world time.
A "Once / Encounter" Ability can be used once, and then you must wait until the next Encounter to use it again. You at any point may ask the Quest Master if the current Encounter is the same or a different one.
Abilities.Duration: Duration on Abilities is usually self-explanatory.
Abilities.Abiliy Requirements:
Abilities may have requirements to use. This is noted with an {Color('orange', 'orange text')} in the tags section of the Ability (e.g. Action Points cost, Cooldown, Requirement, Range, etc).
The most common requirement is "Only usable in Worthy Combat", which can't be cast outside of Combat.
For what a Worthy Combat is, see the Worthy Combat section of these rules.
Abilities.Ability Replacement/Upgrade:
You will encounter Abilities that replace other Abilities. This is noted with a {Color('blue', 'blue text')} in the tags section of the Ability (e.g. Action Points cost, Cooldown, Replacement, Range, etc).
If an Ability you have says "Replaces X", then you don't need to look at the replaced Ability anymore. This is mostly for convenience, so you don't need to clutter your Hero Sheet/Ability Sheet with extra Abilities you will no longer use.
The "My Character" section of the Character Creator automatically hides replaced Abilities.

Some Abilities replace other Abilities, and will list both "Requires X" and "Replaces X".
In that case, you need to already have picked the required/replaced Ability. That Ability still counts as a picked Talent if it's a Talent!
For example, let's say you picked Hail as a Warlock. At a higher Level, there is an Ability called Hail Torrent, which requires and replaces Hail. If you choose to get this, you must still have Hail in your build, and don't get a free different pick for a Class Talent at Level 1!
Abilities.Triggering Abilities:
Some Abilities give you free uses of other Abilities. For example, Clerics get to cast Awe for free, even if it's on a Cooldown.
When an Ability tells you that you can "freely cast X ignoring its Cooldown/Cost", you can cast that Ability in that moment, whether it's on Cooldown or not.
If it's not on Cooldown, the Ability does NOT go on Cooldown if you trigger a free cast like this.
If it's on Cooldown, the Ability remains on Cooldown.
Abilities.Spells:
A Spell is an Ability made with magic.
All Spells are Abilities, but only some Abilities are Spells. This only matters in certain niche scenarios.

There is no limit to how many Spells you can use per Turn.
Abilities.Mana:
Many Classes in the game use a system of points called Mana Points.
You have a number of Mana Points that you can spend to cast some Spells, and you regain all Mana Points back when you start a new Adventure.
Even many non-spellcaster Classes use Mana.

The amount of Mana a Spell costs to cast is represented by the _blue flame_ icon and the number near it.
Each Spell specifies if and how many Mana Points it costs to cast. If you decide to cast Healing Surge, you must expend one Mana Point. If you don't have enough Mana Points to use an Ability, you simply can't.

You can use the Character Creator tool to keep track of your Mana, on the My Character tab, on the bottom-right of the online character sheet.
If playing with pen-and-paper, you can keep track of your Mana Points on a sheet of paper, with marbles, dice, etc. It is your job to keep track of your Mana Points. Don't cheat!
Abilities.Basic Ability (DEPRECATED): If you ever see the term Basic Ability, contact a developer; this term should no longer exist.
Abilities.Feats:
There exist a set of extra Abilities called Feats (which you can find on the {Feats} page). These usually change how you play your Hero or give you some extra interesting options, but always have a cost attached (usually in Max Health, Mana, Initiative, etc).
You can get as many of these as you can afford.
Feats are optional, and you're not necessarily missing out if you decide to play without Feats.
Abilities.Feat Costs:
If you can't afford to get a Feat (e.g. don't have enough Max Mana to sacrifice), you can't get the Feat.
For example, if a Feat costs 1 Focus but your Focus is already 0 or less, you can't spend Focus to buy the Feat.
No such thing. Spells just require Actions, Mana, etc. As long as your hands are free and are not Silenced, you can cast Spells.
There is also no such thing as maintaining ^concentration^. If a Spell has a delayed effect (e.g. Lightning Storm which strikes again), it happens regardless of whether you are Stunned or incapacitated, unless it specifically says so.

Character Advancement.Leveling Up:
Once your Hero has gone through enough of the story, it Levels Up.
When you Level Up, depending on your Class, you gain:
- Max Health
- Health Regen
- +1 in a Stat of choice (up to a limit, detailed below)
- 1 Talent from your new Level's tier
Based on your Class, you may also get:
- +1 Mana
Character Advancement.Leveling Up By Milestone:
The recommended way to Level Up characters is by reaching an important milestone in the story - after completing a quest, defeating a certain boss, etc.
The Quest Master will let you know when you Level Up by milestone.
The recommended number of sessions required to get to the next Level is equal to the current Level.
For example, reaching from Level 1 to Level 2 would require 1 session, from Level 2 to Level 3 - 2 sessions, and so on.
Character Advancement.Leveling Up By Experience:
You might also Level Up your Heroes based on Experience Points.
To get to the next Level, you need to get more Experience Points equal to 100 times the next Level.
For example, reaching from Level 1 to Level 2 would require 200 Experience Points, from Level 2 to Level 3 - 300 Experience Points, and so on.

Defeating enemies awards Experience Points. After winning a Combat, the Quest Master distributes the sum of Experience Points of all enemies defeated, and equally distributes it to the Heroes.
More details on Enemy Experience in the rules for balancing a Combat Encounter.

The Quest Master might also award Experience Points for roleplaying, exploration, etc.
Character Advancement.Talents:
Every Level, your Class gives you a Talent to pick from multiple available Talents.
All Talents are Abilities.

All Classes have Talent tiers for all Levels from 1 to 10.
Starting even from Level 1 and when you reach a certain Level, you get one of the available Talents from that Level's Talent Tiers for free.
If there are multiple Talent Tiers for that Level, you can pick one from each (see Talent Clarifications).

There are 2 Talent Types: Race Talents (given by the Race) and Class Talents (given by the Class).
Character Advancement.Minor and Utility Talents:
Minor and Utility Talents are Abilities that are usually extra things you can do in and outside Combat.
Aside from the free 1 Talent for each Talent tier, you may pick an extra number of Minor and/or Utility Talents equal to your Focus.
Potentially, you could have all Class Talents from a certain Level!
Character Advancement.Relearning/Unlearning/Respeccing:
All Classes can unlearn and re-learn their Talents inbetween Adventures.

Inbetween Adventures, Heroes can "respec their Talents", meaning they can change any of their Talent Choices, freely.
When unlearning a Talent, the Hero loses te passive benefits of that Talent (e.g. Talents that state something like "You have +1 something...").
However, you keep all permanent bonuses a Talent gave you if they are explicitly called "permanent".

Character Stats, Specializations, Quirks and Feats generally can't be changed, unless the Quest Master allows for this in special circumstances, with things such as a Tome of Unlearning item or undergoing intensive training for a period of time, to retrain the character's capabilities.
There are, however, options to change some of these. You can view them at the Game menu, under Other, on the Shop & Prices page.

Items.Items (using items):
Most items you can use in combat take 1 Action Point to make (e.g. Scrolls, Potions, Caltrops, etc).
Even if an Ability normally takes 0 Action Points, the scroll still takes 1 Action Point to use. For example, if you have a Scroll of Smite, you must first land a weapon attack, then use the scroll to add the extra Damage (just like Smite says, but with 1 Action Point).
There might be situations in which using a Scroll is not feasible.
Items.Potions:
Consuming a Potion takes a 1 Action Point.

Every Unit can safely use at most one "Potion" per in-game hour. If a brew restores Health, Mana, Movement, etc (e.g. is not a lasting buff), it counts as a "Potion". Magical foods with similar properties count as Potions. The Quest Master can choose to rule something as "not a Potion", which means it can be safely consumed, as per the item's rules.    
The second Potion consumed per hour makes the Unit suffer of Exhaustion for 1 hour.
The third and all further Potions consumed per hour make the user pass a Grade 12 Might Check or fall to 0 Health and fall in a coma (Unconscious) for 1 hour.
Items.Scrolls:
A scroll is usually a piece of parchment that has a Spell infused in it. When used, the Scroll releases that Spell and the scroll destroyed. Scrolls are one-time use items.
Using a Scroll takes 1 Action Point
You don't need to be a spellcaster to use a Scroll, or expend Mana. Scrolls ignore cooldowns on your Abilities - they have nothing to do with your own Ability Cooldowns or Costs.

When using a scroll, you use your own Stats for that Spell (e.g. your Focus, your Presence, etc).
The scroll Spell does not benefit from effect bonuses increased by your Hero's Levels or by Talents. It is simply a plain copy of a Spell.
Items.Magic Item Shop:
As a Quest Master, be careful with how you allow Players to buy scrolls from Shops! Players should not be able to buy all the scrolls they need and stock up on, say, 6 Fireball Scrolls they can just use on a whim.
Shop stocks should be limited to a few different scrolls and potions to buy.
Items.Magic Items and Soulbound:
Magic items are powered by the soul of their carrier!
Once a magic item is equipped or used, it becomes Soulbound to that character until the end of the Adventure. An item that is Soulbound to a Unit has no effect in someone else's hand, does not provide any benefit other than the default ones if it's an armor, and acts as a regular weapon if it's a weapon.
Items.Armor Slots: All armor you buy from the standard Armors page fits the upper and lower body. You can only have 1 armor piece fit that specific body part, without overlapping. There are theoretic slots for: - Head - Legs - Feet - Hands & arms You can also wear as many rings, necklaces, etc as you want, within reason. Only Magic Items can provide extra Combat benefits when equipped into these slots. Equipping a non-magic helmet, for example, will not give extra benefits, but it may look menacing!
Items.Don/Doff Armor:
At the start of each Adventure, you decide what armor you want to have equipped. It can not be unequipped for the rest of the Adventure except for a ^worthy reason^, such as unequipping an armor set to replace it with a different newly acquired one.
For example, it is not a ^worthy reason^ to unequip a plate armor to equip a robe that grants +1 History so you can roll that Check with the bonus, then to reequip the Plate.

Non-Combat and Time.Checks:
Whenever a Unit wants to do something that's not guaranteed to succeed (e.g. jumping over a chasm), the Unit rolls 2d6 and adds one fitting Stat (Might, Instinct, Focus, etc). Generaly, the Quest Master will call out for a Unit to roll a Check to determine whether they succeed at it.
If the Unit any Skills that fit the Check, they may add those to the roll, gaining a +1 for each. Non-Heroes don't usually have Skills.
Non-Combat and Time.Skills:
Your Hero has Skills that can further add a bonus to your Checks!

Skills are like _tags_ your Hero has. Each Skill may give you a +1 to a Check, if it makes sense for that specific Check. You can add multiple Skills to the same Check, if it makes sense.
For example, let's say you want to remove a fallen tree from the road. Baseline, this would a Check with 2d6 + your Might. But if you have, say, the Lifting and Lumberjacking Skills, you can add +1 for each!

^However^, you may not add multiple Skills that overlap too much, by common sense! For example, if you have Legwork and Jumping, one could argue Legwork automatically includes Jumping, so you would not be able to add both to the same Check.
Also, the same Skill does not add with itself. Having the Jumping Skill twice does not increase your bonus.

^You have a number of Skills^ equal to your Focus + 2, and you can spend 3 Plot Points to get a new Skill.
^Important note:^ whenever you acquire a new Skill, it must be a ^one-word tag^ (unless it's from a special Ability or magic item)!
Non-Combat and Time.Flaws:
Flaws are just like Skills, but negative: one word tags that may give a -1 to a Check (e.g. Anxious, Injured, IBS). But there is an important distinction.
^Flaws are not automatically added to Checks.^ Instead, _you choose when to add a Flaw to a Check_ (for a -1).
If you added a Flaw and still succeeded, your team gets a Plot Point. If you failed, the Quest Master gets a Plot Point.

You can add as many Flaws as it makes sense to the Check and that many Plot Points will be produced.

^You have 3 Flaws^, and you may acquire more through Quirks (at the end of an Adventure), Abilities, or special situations.

_Note that it is in your advantage to have Flaws, so you have more opportunities to generate Plot Points!_
Non-Combat and Time.Helping Check:
When someone is about to make a Check, you may commit to helping them before they roll.

First, make the same Check yourself, using at least one extra Skill and one extra Flaw that aren't already being used for the main Check. As usual, they must make sense for how you're helping.

If you succeed, add the extra Skills you used to the main Check. If you fail, add the extra Flaws you used instead.

Only the main Check produces Plot Points. The extra Skills and Flaws contributed by different characters follow the normal rules: they can't overlap too much.
Non-Combat and Time.Repeating Checks:
Focus Checks normally can't be repeated - if one fails an Focus, then they simply don't know, aren't able to comprehend it no matter how hard they try, or can't sense what they're supposed to.
If the main Check, with or without help doesn't know something, it becomes very unlikely that someone else knows it.
Might Checks normally can't be repeated unless the character tries a different approach (up to the Quest Master's interpretation).
Instinct and Presence Checks may sometimes be repeated, but, normally, the failure is more disrupting.
Non-Combat and Time.Leading Checks and Helping:
If multiple players want to make the same Check (e.g. inspecting for traps, remembering informatio, etc), determine (the Quest Master or the players) which Hero is the most qualified for it.
Only the most qualified character rolls the Check.
Other Heroes may try to roll a Helping Check, to help the character rolling the main Check.
Non-Combat and Time.Adventure:
An Adventure is a period of gameplay defined by the Quest Master. An Adventure could be one full dungeon, one quest, one session, or just one day outdoors adventuring.
Heroes regain all resources (Health, Mana, Cooldowns, etc) at the end of an Adventure (inbetween Adventures).

For combat purposes, it is recommended that an Adventure contain 3 Medium-difficulty combats (or 2 difficult ones). Combat difficulty is calculated by the Quest Master via total Monster Experience (see Monsters).

Heroes can also "respec" inbetween Adventures - can choose different Talents and known Abilities.
There is no concept of "long resting" in Questguard - you only regain spent resources inbetween Adventures.

The Quest Master decides what contstitutes an Adventure, and it's the Quest Master's job to pace Adventures properly as to give Heroes an adequate challenge or fair checkpoints. Also, the Quest Master may or may not tell the Heroes how long the Adventure is, or when it ends.
Non-Combat and Time.Quest:
The Quest System is an alterntive to the Adventure System (tentative).

A completed Quest (or Sidequest) is a milestone for the players. When the players reach that milestone in the story (complete a Quest), they regain all resources.
In short, Players regain all resources upon completing a Quest. Players Heal for an amount equal to their Health Regen when completing a Sidequest.
The Quest Master decides what a Completed Quest or Sidequest is - it could be the end of a dungeon, saving someone, or finishing the game session.

For combat purposes, it is recommended that a Quest contain a total of 3 Medium-difficulty combats (or 2 difficult ones), assuming no Sidequests. Combat difficulty is calculated by the Quest Master via total Monster Experience (see Monsters).

Players can relearn Abilities and Talents after completing a Quest.
A Quest may or can't have a clearly defined start or end.
As a QM, feel free to say a Quest is complete whenever you feel the players need to recover their resources. If the players ask "Was this a quest?" you have the option to say "It was a Sidequest".
Non-Combat and Time.Encounter:
An Encounter is a continuous challenge. Most Combats are Encounters, but social, exploration, stealth, or chase scenes can also be encounters.
Entering Combat may not necessarily be a different encounter. If the Heroes are exploring a dark cave and they get ambushed by giant bats, then defeat the bats and resume exploring, this entire sequence might constitute only 1 encounter.

The Quest Master decides what contstitutes an Encounter, and it's the Quest Master's job determine the length of Encounters properly as to give Heroes an adequate challenge or fair checkpoints. Also, the Quest Master may or may not tell the Heroes how long the Encounter is, or when it ends.
Non-Combat and Time.Combat Grace Period:
For 10 minutes after finishing a combat encounter, all Units who participated are still considered in combat.
Some Abilities and game mechanics (e.g. Health Regen) require you to be out of combat to use.
Be on your toes for a while after finishing a fight!
